# Isaiah 39 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview

Isaiah 39 forms a historical bridge between the first part of Isaiah (chapters 1–38, dealing mainly with the Assyrian threat) and the second part (chapters 39–66, prophetically addressing the coming Babylonian captivity). It records Hezekiah's foolish display of wealth to Babylonian envoys, Isaiah's confrontation, the prophecy of exile, and Hezekiah's self-centered response. The parallel passage is 2 Kings 20:12–19.

— Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-39/

---

## v. 1: "At that time Merodach-baladan son of Baladan king of Babylon sent letters and a gift to Hezekiah, for he had heard about Hezekiah's illness and recovery."

- **"At that time"** links this event directly to Hezekiah's miraculous recovery and the fifteen additional years granted by God (Isa 38). A moment of spiritual victory becomes a moment of spiritual testing. 2 Chronicles 32:31 explicitly states that God "left him alone only to test him, that He might know all that was in his heart." (Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-39-commentary)

- **Merodach-baladan** (also called Berodach-baladan in 2 Kings 20:12) was a Chaldean rebel king who fought against Assyrian domination of Babylon. He ruled 721–710 BC and again 703–702 BC. The embassy was not merely a goodwill visit; it was a political attempt to draw Judah into an anti-Assyrian alliance. The "present" (gift), interpreted according to Eastern customs, "would seem almost like an acknowledgment of Hezekiah's hegemony, or even suzerainty, in such a confederacy." (Ellicott: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-39.html; also Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/39.htm)

- The stated pretext — concern for Hezekiah's health — masks the real motive: intelligence-gathering and alliance-building. "After great spiritual deliverance often comes subtle spiritual danger: flattery, attention, and worldly admiration can test faith just as severely as suffering does." (Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-39-commentary)

- Gill notes that Merodach-baladan's name incorporates three idol names — Merodach (a Babylonian god), Bal (contraction of Baal), and Adon (Adonis). (Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/39.htm)

---

## v. 2: "And Hezekiah welcomed the envoys gladly and showed them what was in his treasure house—the silver, the gold, the spices, and the precious oil, as well as his entire armory—all that was found in his storehouses. There was nothing in his palace or in all his dominion that Hezekiah did not show them."

- **"Hezekiah was pleased" / "welcomed them gladly"** — The Hebrew verb can carry an arrogant sense (cf. Job 31:29; Ps 35:15; Ezek 25:6). Hezekiah was flattered that a distant power like Babylon would notice him. "Judah was a lowly nation with little power, and Babylon was a junior superpower. To receive this notice and recognition…must have really made Hezekiah feel he was important." (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-39/)

- **The display of treasures** went far beyond normal hospitality. There is no evidence the Babylonians asked to see the treasures; Hezekiah volunteered the tour. "Hezekiah carries out an act of self-display rather than careful stewardship of God's gifts." His failure was "turning blessings into trophies." (Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-39-commentary)

- **A five-fold repetition of "his"** in the original emphasizes Hezekiah's childish self-display. The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary notes: "Here is an amazing contrast: the ambassadors of the Assyrian set Hezekiah to praying; those of Babylon set him to proud boasting!" (Garner-Howes: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/isaiah-39.html)

- **What about the chronology?** Ellicott notes this fixes the date prior to Hezekiah's payment to Sennacherib (2 Kings 18:15–16), unless the treasury was replenished by spoils from the destroyed Assyrian army. "The display was obviously something more than the ostentation of a Crœsus showing his treasures to Solon. It was practically a display of the resources of the kingdom, intended to impress the Babylonian ambassadors with a sense of his importance as an ally." (Ellicott: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-39.html)

- **The spiritual problem**: Hezekiah was "in the dangerous place of wanting to please and impress men, especially ungodly men." Paul wrote, "If I still pleased men, I would not be a bondservant of Christ" (Gal 1:10). Hezekiah "is no longer a true servant of God." Motyer suggests what Hezekiah should have said: "'Thank you for coming…but the fact is I have a divine promise to lean on; it has been confirmed personally in my return to health and cosmically in the sign of the sun. I cannot turn from faith in the promises of God.'" (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-39/)

- **Matthew Henry** offers seven practical lessons from this verse, including: "It is a hard matter to keep the spirit low in the midst of great advancements," and "We have need to watch over our own spirits when we are showing our friends our possessions." (Henry, cited at https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/isaiah-39.html)

- **The irony**: The very things God had miraculously delivered from Assyria are now visually handed over to Babylon. "What grace had preserved, pride now exposes." (Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-39-commentary)

---

## vv. 3–4: "Then the prophet Isaiah went to King Hezekiah and asked, 'Where did those men come from, and what did they say to you?' 'They came to me from a distant land,' Hezekiah replied, 'from Babylon.' 'What have they seen in your palace?' Isaiah asked. 'They have seen everything in my palace,' answered Hezekiah. 'There is nothing among my treasures that I did not show them.'"

- **Isaiah comes uninvited** — the prophet's boldness in confronting the king is characteristic of the prophetic office (cf. 2 Sam 12; 1 Kings 13; 2 Chron 16:7–9). The Pulpit Commentary notes: "This bold attitude was one which prophets were entitled to take by virtue of their office, which called upon them to bear testimony, even before kings, and to have no respect of persons." Isaiah comes "unsent for, to rebuke the king." (Pulpit: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/39.htm)

- **Isaiah's questions** were almost certainly rhetorical — he already knew the answers. "It is likely that his questions were guided by God to allow Hezekiah the opportunity to answer honestly (which he did) and to see his error himself (which he apparently did not)." (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-39/)

- **Hezekiah dodges the first question** — "What did these men say?" He never answers it, but eagerly answers the second: they came "from a far country, from Babylon." Gill observes: "he makes no answer to the first question, but at once replies to the second, as being what his heart was lifted up with; that ambassadors should come to him from a very distant country." (Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/39.htm)

- **"A far country"** — Hezekiah seems to boast about the distance traveled. "The phrase suggests pride. The distance they came magnifies the honor." Notably, "there is no textual evidence that he ever even mentioned Yahweh and how the LORD has delivered Judah from the Assyrians." (Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-39-commentary)

- **"They have seen everything"** — Hezekiah's response shows no shame, no discernment. "There is the sense that Hezekiah was proud to tell Isaiah this. He is like a small-town boy who is awed by the attention of a big-city man." His confession of full disclosure almost seems boastful: "The problem is not dishonesty but indiscretion (and stupidity). Hezekiah's failure was not deception, but prideful transparency before the wrong audience." (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-39/; Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-39-commentary)

---

## vv. 5–7: "Then Isaiah said to Hezekiah, 'Hear the word of the LORD of Hosts: The time will surely come when everything in your palace and all that your fathers have stored up until this day will be carried off to Babylon. Nothing will be left, says the LORD. And some of your descendants, your own flesh and blood, will be taken away to be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.'"

- **"Hear the word of the LORD of Hosts"** — The imperative "Hear" (*shama*) echoes the covenant language of the Shema (Dt 6:4). It demands "attention, submission, and obedience," not mere listening. "Isaiah is not making a suggestion inviting discussion or giving an explanation but is summoning Hezekiah to receive the divine word without argument or defense." (Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-39-commentary; Bible.org: https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-39)

- **"LORD of Hosts"** — Gill notes the significance: "a greater King than thou art, who art so elated with thy riches, and grandeur, and fame; or than the king of Babylon, whose ambassadors these are; even the King of kings, and Lord of armies above and below." (Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/39.htm)

- **The judgment fits the crime** — "Measure for measure" (Jarchi, cited by Gill): because Hezekiah showed everything, everything would be taken. Because he displayed it to Babylon, it would be carried to Babylon. (Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/39.htm)

- **Predictive prophecy**: This is "the first explicit reference to the Babylonian captivity in Isaiah." Critics who reject predictive prophecy have used this verse to argue for a later date of writing. But as the Pulpit Commentary argues: "To suppose that Isaiah foresaw by mere human wisdom the Babylonian conquest of Judaea…is to give him credit for a sagacity quite unexampled and psychologically impossible. The kingdom of Babylon was one among many that were struggling hard to maintain independence against the grasping and encroaching Assyria…Nothing short of the true prophetic afflatus, which is God the Holy Ghost speaking by the mouth of his servants, could have made such an anticipation." (Pulpit: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/39.htm; Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-39.html)

- **Fulfillment**: The treasures were carried to Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar in 586 BC (2 Kings 24:13; 25:13–15; 2 Chron 36:18; Jer 20:5). Ellicott notes a twofold fulfillment: (1) Hezekiah's son Manasseh was carried prisoner to Babylon by Esar-haddon (2 Chron 33:11); (2) the final exile under Jehoiachin, and the taking of Daniel and his companions "of the king's seed and of the princes" into the Babylonian court (Daniel 1:3–4). (Ellicott: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-39.html)

- **"Your descendants…will be eunuchs"** — This was worse than losing material treasure; Hezekiah would lose his "true riches" — his own flesh and blood. Many commentators link this to Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, who were taken into the palace of the king of Babylon and were likely made eunuchs (placed under "the master of the eunuchs," Dan 1:3). (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-39/; Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/39.htm)

- Some Jewish commentators (Kimchi, Ben Melech) interpret "eunuchs" more broadly as "princes" or "officials" (Gill, citing the Targum). But the literal sense is predominant in most Protestant commentaries.

---

## v. 8: "But Hezekiah said to Isaiah, 'The word of the LORD that you have spoken is good.' For he thought, 'At least there will be peace and security in my lifetime.'"

- **Two main interpretations of Hezekiah's response** exist among commentators:

  **A. A negative, self-centered response** (majority Protestant view): Hezekiah shows relief that judgment is deferred. "God announces coming judgment, and all he can respond with is relief that it will not happen in his lifetime." He is "almost the exact opposite of an 'others-centered' person. He is almost totally self-centered. All he cares about is his own personal comfort and success." David Guzik compares this unfavorably to David's response in 2 Samuel 24:17: "I have sinned and done wickedly; but these sheep, what have they done? Let thy hand, I pray thee, be against me, and against my father's house." Ellicott says Hezekiah's words "have the appearance of a pious resignation, but we feel that they are less true and noble than those of David" and "remind us a little too much of 'Après moi le déluge.'" (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-39/; Ellicott: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-39.html)

  **B. A positive, submissive response** (minority view): Hezekiah humbly accepts God's judgment as just and is thankful for mercy in the delay. Gill takes this view: "Hezekiah was at once convinced of his sin, acknowledged it and repented of it, and owned that the sentence pronounced was but just and right; and that there was a mixture of mercy and goodness in it, in that time was given, and it was not immediately executed." Haydock's Catholic Commentary similarly defends Hezekiah: "He is not unconcerned about his children, but dares not request more. Having given way to immoderate joy and vanity, he was informed that all his treasures should be taken away." Matthew Henry likewise reads it more charitably: Hezekiah shows "penitent and patient submission to this sentence." (Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/39.htm; Haydock: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/isaiah-39.html; Henry, cited at https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/isaiah-39.html)

  **C. Some scholars** suggest Hezekiah's happiness stems from learning he will have a son (since the prophecy mentions "sons who will issue from you, whom you will beget"), implying that the prophecy indirectly promises him an heir. (Bible.org: https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-39)

- **"Peace and truth"** (*shalom* and *'emeth*) — The word "truth" here has the sense of "stability" or "security" (cf. Ps 54:5). Jeremiah 14:13 uses the same pairing with the meaning "assured peace." (Ellicott: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-39.html)

- **Hezekiah did not finish well**. Though he started as an outstandingly godly king (2 Kings 18:3–7), his beginning was better than his end. God gave him fifteen extra years, "but the added years did not make him a better or more godly man." Time alone does not sanctify — only how we use it. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-39/)

- **Dr. Constable** (Evangelical/Dispensational) sums up the broader lesson: "During this period Hezekiah trusted God twice and failed to trust God once. This should teach us that it is possible for a person to trust God in very difficult circumstances and turn right around and trust in people and things with the next temptation." (Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-39.html)

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

The main interpretive divide among Protestant sources concerns **v. 8 — Hezekiah's response**:

| Tradition | Reading of v. 8 | Source |
|-----------|----------------|--------|
| **Pentecostal/Charismatic** (Guzik, Enduring Word) | Strongly negative: Hezekiah is self-centered, relieved only that judgment comes after his lifetime | https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-39/ |
| **Baptist (Gill)** | Positive/submissive: Hezekiah repented, acknowledged the justice of the sentence, and was grateful for delay | https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/39.htm |
| **Baptist (Garner-Howes)** | Negative: Hezekiah "failed the test," his heart was lifted up in pride | https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/isaiah-39.html |
| **Anglican (Ellicott)** | Negative/unfavorable compared to David; "Après moi le déluge" | https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-39.html |
| **Broad Evangelical (Matthew Henry)** | Positive: "penitent and patient submission" | https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/isaiah-39.html |
| **Evangelical/Dispensational (Constable)** | Negative: "deeply disappointing" compared to Hezekiah's earlier repentance in chapter 38 | https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-39.html |

Beyond v. 8, the traditions are broadly united on the core meaning: Hezekiah's display was an act of pride, it represented misplaced trust in political alliances rather than God, and Isaiah's prophecy authentically predicts the Babylonian exile.

---

## Other Views

### Catholic Reading

- **Haydock's Catholic Commentary** (1811) is brief but notably defends Hezekiah in v. 8: he is "not unconcerned about his children, but dares not request more." The fault was "immoderate joy and vanity," but his response to the sentence is one of submission, not callousness. (Haydock: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/isaiah-39.html)

### Modern Critical Scholarship

- **The issue of predictive prophecy**: Bible.org and Constable both note that critics who reject supernatural predictive prophecy use the explicit naming of Babylon in Isaiah 39:6 as evidence for a late (exilic or post-exilic) date for this section of Isaiah. Conservative commentators respond that this is unwarranted skepticism and that the prophecy is exactly what it claims to be — a supernatural revelation from God through Isaiah. (Bible.org: https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-39; Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-39.html; Pulpit: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/39.htm)

- **The chapter as a bridge**: Many scholars recognize Isaiah 39 as the hinge between "First Isaiah" (Assyrian period) and "Second Isaiah" (Babylonian/exilic perspective). This is acknowledged by both conservative (Guzik) and critical commentators.

---

## Key Application Themes

1. **Pride after blessing**: "After great spiritual deliverance often comes subtle spiritual danger: flattery, attention, and worldly admiration can test faith just as severely as suffering does." (Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-39-commentary)

2. **God tests the heart**: 2 Chronicles 32:31 explicitly frames this as a divine test. "God left him alone only to test him, that He might know all that was in his heart." Success in one trial does not guarantee faithfulness in the next.

3. **Pleasing men vs. serving God**: "When we live to please men, we cannot at the same time live to please and serve God." (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-39/)

4. **Finishing well**: Extra time, extra resources, and extra blessings only matter if we use them to serve God. Hezekiah's added fifteen years produced his worst moment. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-39/)
